opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the most useful way to think about it starts with what networks learn first. There's a lot of evidence for what you could call a distributional simplicity bias: early in training, networks mostly pick up the low-order statistics of each class, like the mean of the images and then the covariance, how pixels co-vary. Only later do they start using higher-order structure, the kind of shapes and parts we'd recognize as the actual object.

If that's right, then early in training the network is behaving roughly like a linear or quadratic classifier on those low-order statistics. And those classifiers are very easy to fool with tiny perturbations. You find directions in pixel space where the class means or covariances differ, maybe directions with very little variance in natural images, and you nudge the image a small amount along them. To a human it looks identical, because we don't see the world through those statistics. But to a model leaning heavily on them, that small nudge carries a lot of evidence for the wrong class.

So in a sense, the early adversarial examples aren't mysterious. They tell you what features the model is actually using at that point. One test is to take an image and edit only its low-order statistics, shifting the mean and covariance toward another class while leaving everything else alone. If an early-training network gets fooled by that but a later checkpoint doesn't, you've learned something about how its reliance on features shifts during training.

I think this connects to the broader view that adversarial vulnerability is less a weird bug and more a symptom of models using features that are genuinely predictive but not the ones we care about. Early in training, those features are mostly the simple statistical ones. Robustness then partly comes down to whether, and how much, the model moves beyond them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses perturbations that fool networks, but does not say they differ from adversarial examples because they were not optimized against the network.

r002.rationale: It says early networks rely on simple low-order statistics such as means and covariances, and that humans do not perceive images through those statistics.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we looked at in a fair amount of detail, and I think the picture that emerges is actually pretty clean once you think about it in terms of what the network is capable of representing at each point in training.

So early in training, the network is basically a linear model, or close to it. There's a lot of work on this, the whole simplicity bias literature, and what we found is that in the first few hundred or thousand steps, a network trained on image classification is essentially doing something very close to what a linear classifier on raw pixels would do. It's picking up on things like average color, overall brightness, very coarse low-frequency statistics of the image.

And once you know that, the adversarial examples basically explain themselves. If your model is a linear function of the pixels, then the perturbation that moves the output the most per unit of norm is just the gradient, which for a linear model is a fixed direction in pixel space. And that direction tends to be this very smooth, low-frequency thing, because that's what the early model is sensitive to. So you can take an image, add a tiny amount of this low-frequency pattern, and to a human it looks identical, because humans are not doing linear classification on raw pixel intensities. We're looking at edges and shapes and objects. But to the early network, you've shifted the one or two statistics it actually cares about, and that's enough to flip the label.

What I think is interesting is that this is kind of the opposite of the story people usually tell about adversarial examples in trained networks, where the worry is that the model has latched onto some high-frequency, non-robust feature that's genuinely predictive but imperceptible to us. Early in training it's not that. The model hasn't found any subtle features yet. It's just that it's a very low-capacity function, and a low-capacity function has a lot of inputs it can't distinguish between, so it's cheap to walk from one class region to another.

And then as training goes on, you see the adversarial perturbations change character. They go from these broad smooth blobs to something much more textured and high-frequency, which tracks the network moving up the spectrum, so to speak, from low-order to higher-order features. So you can almost read the adversarial examples as a diagnostic of what the model is representing at that point. I find that a much more useful framing than treating them as some mysterious pathology.

r001.rationale: The response describes gradient-based adversarial perturbations, but does not identify lack of optimization against the network as the distinguishing feature of the image modifications.

r002.rationale: It says early networks rely on simple statistics such as average color, brightness, and low-frequency features, while humans rely on edges, shapes, and objects.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful way to understand this is that looking unchanged to us doesn’t mean the image is unchanged in every way that matters for prediction. Our visual system ignores a lot of information that a neural network can pick up on.

You can have a very small change spread across thousands of pixels, and those changes can add up coherently for the network even though we don’t notice them. In a local, linear approximation, you’re moving the input in a direction that changes the model’s score very quickly, while keeping the change to each individual pixel tiny.

And that doesn’t require a fully trained model. Even early in training, the network has directions it’s sensitive to. A perturbation tailored to its current parameters can exploit those sensitivities. That doesn’t necessarily mean the same perturbation will keep working as training proceeds, or work on another network. But it illustrates the gap between perceptual similarity for humans and similarity according to the model.

r001.rationale: The response says the perturbation is tailored to the network’s current parameters, but does not identify lack of optimization against the network as the distinction from adversarial examples.

r002.rationale: The response describes information the network can detect that humans may miss and mentions early sensitivity, but does not specify simple image features that humans rely on much less.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful way to understand adversarial examples is that looking unchanged to us doesn’t mean the image is unchanged in ways that matter to the network. Our visual system ignores lots of small variations, but the network hasn’t necessarily learned those same invariances.

In a high-dimensional input space, you can make a very small change to lots of pixels, and those changes can collectively have a large effect on the output. Locally, you can think of the network as approximately linear: if you move each pixel a little bit in a direction that increases the loss, all those little contributions can add up.

And that mechanism doesn’t require a fully trained network. Early in training, the model already has directions in input space that it’s sensitive to, even if those directions don’t correspond to meaningful visual features. So I wouldn’t interpret the effect as necessarily exploiting some sophisticated concept the network has learned. You can get it from the geometry of the model and its sensitivity to inputs before it has learned very much at all.

r001.rationale: The response discusses adversarial examples and network-sensitive changes, but never says the modifications were made without optimizing against the network.

r002.rationale: It says early networks have sensitive directions that may not be meaningful visual features, but does not identify simple image features that humans depend on much less.
